concepts.decision: Use it to locate the affected function and control, while recognizing real protocols can span layers.
concepts.definition: Seven-layer reference model for locating communication functions, controls, and faults.
concepts.failureExample: Calling an application authorization flaw a Layer 3 issue directs remediation to routing.
concepts.label: Osi Model

concepts.decision: Use it to reason about deployed Internet protocols; translate, rather than equate blindly, to OSI terms.
concepts.definition: Implementation-oriented stack that groups networking functions into fewer protocol layers.
concepts.failureExample: Assuming TCP/IP and OSI layers map one-for-one obscures where encryption or routing terminates.
concepts.label: Tcp Ip Model

concepts.decision: Define zones and enforce/observe every required crossing using policy that matches the actual flow.
concepts.definition: Physical or logical restriction of communication between network groups to reduce reachability and blast radius.
concepts.failureExample: A separate VLAN has an unrestricted routed path into a sensitive subnet.
concepts.label: Network Segmentation

concepts.decision: Use when east-west blast radius matters and maintain explicit service identity, policy, and observability.
concepts.definition: Fine-grained workload or identity-aware policy enforced close to services rather than only at large network zones.
concepts.failureExample: A broad subnet rule lets one compromised host laterally reach every workload in the segment.
concepts.label: Micro Segmentation

concepts.decision: Allow only flows with known purpose, source/destination identity, protocol, path, and monitoring point.
concepts.definition: Documented north-south and east-west communications among users, services, management, and dependencies.
concepts.failureExample: An undocumented east-west path lets a compromised workload reach a sensitive service.
concepts.label: Traffic Flows

concepts.decision: Separate and protect planes where risk warrants, especially management identities and control interfaces.
concepts.definition: Data plane forwards traffic; control plane decides forwarding; management plane configures and administers devices.
concepts.failureExample: A protected data path still fails if an attacker reconfigures it through the management plane.
concepts.label: Network Planes

concepts.decision: Collect protected, actionable signals at enforcement and management points without creating an unmanaged collector path.
concepts.definition: Flow, fault, capacity, and policy telemetry that lets operators detect and explain network behavior.
concepts.failureExample: Encryption or segmentation failures remain invisible when denied flows and device health are not observed.
concepts.label: Network Observability

concepts.decision: Choose by protected traffic, termination points, key/certificate validation, metadata exposure, inspection, and availability impact.
concepts.definition: Protocols selected for a specific layer, endpoint identity, confidentiality, integrity, and failure model.
concepts.failureExample: Selecting “encryption” without locating endpoints leaves an onward path unprotected.
concepts.label: Secure Protocols

concepts.decision: Match authentication, segmentation, monitoring, and physical/radio risks to the wireless use case.
concepts.definition: Controls for radio association, encryption, admission, rogue detection, management, and RF availability.
concepts.failureExample: A strong Wi-Fi password does not isolate guest or IoT traffic from enterprise services.
concepts.label: Wireless Security

concepts.decision: Protect controller identity, policy changes, APIs, availability, logs, and rollback as a high-value control plane.
concepts.definition: Architecture that separates/centralizes programmable network control from forwarding devices through software control interfaces.
concepts.failureExample: A compromised SDN controller can alter policy across many forwarding devices.
concepts.label: Software Defined Networking

concepts.decision: Choose physical, VLAN/VRF/VPN, or workload policy boundary from the required reduction in available paths and operational constraints.
concepts.definition: Explicit physical or logical separation point whose crossing must be controlled and observed.
concepts.failureExample: A cable-sharing “separate” path bypasses the assumed physical boundary.
concepts.label: Physical Logical Boundary

misconceptions.claim: A firewall at the perimeter makes internal segmentation unnecessary.
misconceptions.correction: East-west movement, cloud paths, wireless, and compromised insiders require internal boundaries and monitoring.

misconceptions.claim: The OSI model tells you exactly where every modern protocol belongs.
misconceptions.correction: It is a conceptual aid; multilayer and tunneled protocols may span or encapsulate layers.

misconceptions.claim: Any encrypted tunnel protects the application end to end.
misconceptions.correction: Protection ends where the selected protocol terminates; proxies, gateways, endpoints, and management paths require separately verified controls.

outcome: Given a network scenario, map the flow and architecture, choose proportionate segmentation and protocol protections, and identify the metrics and monitoring needed to validate the design.

sections.body: The OSI model is a troubleshooting and control vocabulary; TCP/IP groups those functions differently for implementation. IPv4/IPv6 addressing and unicast, broadcast, multicast, and anycast shape reachability. Document north-south and east-west flows, data/control/management planes, and transport choices such as store-and-forward versus cut-through. Capacity decisions require bandwidth, throughput, latency, jitter, and signal-to-noise context because availability and security controls can affect each other.
keyPoints: Models help locate a control or failure; they are not themselves security controls.
Traffic direction and plane separation expose different trust and monitoring needs.
Performance metrics should be tied to an availability or user requirement.
sections.title: Reason about layers, flows, and performance

sections.body: Physical separation includes in-band, out-of-band, and air-gapped designs; logical separation includes VLANs, VPNs, virtual routing and forwarding, and virtual domains. Micro-segmentation applies policy closer to workloads through overlays, distributed firewalls, routers, IDS/IPS, and zero-trust decisions. Edge, VPC, SDN, SD-WAN, NFV, CDN, wireless, cellular, satellite, and converged protocols add dependencies that must be inventoried, authenticated, monitored, and capacity-managed.
keyPoints: Segmentation is useful only when routing, identity, and policy enforcement prevent unintended paths.
Zero trust is a continuous decision model, not a synonym for a VLAN.
Wireless, cellular, CDN, VPC, and SDN boundaries remain part of the security architecture.
sections.title: Reduce blast radius with deliberate boundaries

sections.body: Use secure protocol choices appropriate to the communication purpose: IPSec for network-layer protection, SSH for secure administration, and TLS for protected application sessions are examples. Consider what each protocol authenticates, encrypts, protects against modification, exposes to intermediaries, and logs. Monitoring and management should detect faults, abnormal flow, capacity pressure, and policy violations without creating an unmanaged management path.
keyPoints: Protocol selection depends on endpoint trust, layer, threat, and operational support.
Encryption does not automatically authenticate every endpoint or protect metadata.
Management interfaces and observability pipelines require their own access and integrity controls.
sections.title: Select secure protocols and observability

sections.body: IPsec provides security services at the IP layer and uses security associations, key management, and cryptographic algorithms; SSH protects an administrative transport/session; TLS protects an application session. Do not select only by the word “encryption.” Identify the endpoints that terminate protection, traffic and metadata exposed before/after that boundary, identity/authentication, keys/certificates, policy enforcement point, logging, inspection impact, availability dependency, and failure behavior. A secure tunnel to an untrusted endpoint or unmanaged management plane does not make the protected service trustworthy.
keyPoints: The layer and termination point determine what a channel control can and cannot protect.
Protocol deployment requires policy, key/identity operations, monitoring, and recovery planning.
sections.title: Select a channel control from its protection boundary

title: Design secure network architectures and segmentation

workedExamples.reasoning: Model north-south ingress and east-west service flows separately. Place public ingress behind protected edge controls, isolate management out-of-band or by tightly controlled logical segment, use identity-aware micro-segmentation between tiers, protect service channels with appropriate TLS, and send flow, capacity, and policy events to monitoring. A flat subnet would make compromise of one tier unnecessarily broad.

workedExamples.takeaway: Model north-south ingress and east-west service flows separately. Place public ingress behind protected edge controls, isolate management out-of-band or by tightly controlled logical segment, use identity-aware micro-segmentation between tiers, protect service channels with appropriate TLS, and send flow, capacity, and policy events to monitoring. A flat subnet would make compromise of one tier unnecessarily broad.
